title: From data to a DBMS
lead: Start with a design question: what could go wrong if every feature in an application managed its own data?
goals: Distinguish a database, a DBMS, a schema, and an instance
Explain the three levels of abstraction through an example
Identify the system responsibilities behind a query

sections.title: Data, software, and the library model
sections.html:
A library’s books and loans form a database: an organised collection of data. A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that stores, reads, and updates that collection. Keeping the data and managing changes to it are separate responsibilities.

Data model, schema and instance

A data model supplies concepts for representing data. In the relational model, an attribute is a named column and a tuple is a row. Graph models use vertices and edges; document models use fields. A schema chooses a particular structure within a model: Book(book_id, title) and Loan(book_id, member_id) describe a library’s tables. The current rows are its instance. A shop can use Product and Order in the same relational model with a different schema.

Check: do a library and a shop need different data models?

Worked answer. They can both use the relational model while selecting different schemas and storing different instances.

Read PDF pages 10–19 first; pages 21–35 provide context for the Spring 2026 course. Administrative dates belong to that historical slide edition and are not current submission deadlines.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19 ↗. The worked examples are original.

sections.title: Original design exercise: a neighbourhood library
sections.html:
An original scenario. A library keeps books.csv and loans.csv. Initially, a book has identifier B17 and its loan also refers to B17. Mai changes the identifier in the books file to B017, but the program stops before updating the loans file: the loan still refers to B17, an identifier that no longer exists. Someone else then overwrites loans.csv with an older copy, making a new loan disappear.

  1. Draw the data before and after each write. Identify exactly which relationship is lost.
  2. Write the business rules: every loan must refer to an existing book; assuming each book identifier represents one physical copy, each copy may have only one open loan.
  3. Distinguish a modelling error, an update-procedure error, and an error caused by two people writing concurrently.

Analysis. The rule that a book identifier must exist is a data constraint. Changing a book identifier and updating its related loans should form one transaction, a unit of work containing several operations: either both changes finish, or no partial update remains. Overwriting the current file with an older copy is an access-coordination problem. Later lectures introduce the specific transaction mechanisms.

These failures motivate constraint checking, atomic (all-or-nothing) transactions, and coordinated concurrent writes. A query interface answers new questions without a separate file-processing program for each one; an index can locate a key without a complete file scan. Access controls can distinguish public catalogue data from borrower records. These mechanisms must be configured correctly; choosing a database does not automatically secure an application.

Key takeaway

Changing the file format does not fix update errors. Both CSV and JSON can contain broken references or suffer overwritten changes. The system needs constraint checking, all-or-nothing updates, and coordinated writes.

sections.title: Three views of the same system
sections.html:
An original example. A librarian sees borrowers’ names and due dates; visitors searching the catalogue see only book titles and availability. This is the view level: each user group sees the data relevant to it. At the logical level, we describe the tables and relationships; adding due dates gives a schema such as Book(book_id, title) and Loan(book_id, borrower, due). At the physical level, we decide how records and indexes, the structures that help locate data, are arranged.

Suppose Book currently contains (B017, “Databases”). Adding another book changes the instance. Adding a publication-year column changes the schema: the structure now allows each book to carry information the old schema could not express.

Key takeaway

A schema describes structure; an instance is the current data. Distinguishing these changes helps you decide whether an application needs another data row or a new structure for representing its data.

Ask yourself: should changing the page size, the unit managed during reads and writes, from 4 KiB to 8 KiB force the catalogue application to rewrite its queries? This separation is data independence: changing one level while limiting the effect on the level above. Physical data independence helps keep logical queries stable when storage details change.

Check yourself: at which level do we add a borrower’s email address?

Adding the email field changes the logical description of the data. Its storage offset is a physical detail. Deciding who may see it belongs to view and access-control design.

sections.title: Follow a catalogue request through the DBMS
sections.html:
A visitor asks whether B017 is available. The DBMS finds the Book row and relevant Loan rows, reads that data, and answers. The logical description identifies the related data; the physical description locates its bytes. Moving those bytes should not force the query to change. The mechanisms below preview later lessons.

Preview: layers behind a lookup — Lecture 4 and Lecture 5

Query planning checks meaning and chooses a physical plan: operations to compute the result. Operator execution performs scans, filters, and joins; file/index management locates records. Data is read in pages; a buffer frame is RAM space holding one page. Buffer management tracks frames and chooses unused pages for replacement. Disk-space management maps page IDs to storage and reads/writes them. Concurrency and recovery span these responsibilities, which are not necessarily separate operating-system processes.

For an index lookup whose data page is absent from RAM, file/index management requests the page; buffer management obtains a frame and asks disk-space management to read it; execution examines the record. A cached page avoids that read. Planning chooses the access path; buffering carries out the page request.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 ↗. The worked examples are original.

Preview: workload and layout — Lecture 7

OLTP (online transaction processing) usually means many short transactions, such as the lookup. OLAP (online analytical processing) uses broad queries, such as counting loans by month; HTAP (hybrid transaction/analytical processing) combines both. Disk-oriented and in-memory instead describe storage architecture. A disk-oriented DBMS can cache its working set in RAM even when the database is larger than RAM. An in-memory working set still needs a persistence strategy for durability.

Rows keep an entity’s fields together and tend to suit whole-entity operations; columns group one attribute across entities and tend to suit scans of a few attributes. These tendencies allow both transactions on columns and analysis on rows. Cached pages can avoid disk reads while the DBMS remains disk-oriented. RAM is volatile, losing contents without power; a RAM write alone is not a durable commit.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 11, 12, 13, 14 ↗ · Physical PDF pp. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 11, 12, 16 ↗. The worked examples are original.

Before Lecture 2, write a plain-language library question and its expected answer for three rows. The original exercises here are not official assessed submissions. They progress from data questions and relational expressions to page-I/O costs, buffers/indexes, execution plans, and correct results under concurrency and failures. The expected answer helps check those later methods.

quiz.question: Changing a record’s byte position primarily belongs to which level?
quiz.explanation: A byte position is a physical representation detail; the schema describes the meaning and structure of the data.
